Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
articles.description: Collabora and Nextcloud pitch alternatives as education customers weigh the cost of losing free services
articles.content:
The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.

As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.

A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."

A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.

Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.

"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

articles.title: Breaking Down Theo's Shock Moment in The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 and the Mystery of His Father With Actor Tyroe Muhafidin
articles.description: A spoiler-filled The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 interview with Theo actor Tyroe Muhafidin.
articles.content:
Warning! Spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 Episodes 1-4 follow.

If you’re caught up with The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, you’ll have watched Season 3, Episode 4 and were probably left reeling by a shock character death that leaves the elves in a spot of bother going into the final stretch.

During the first four episodes of Season 3, we see Theo, played by Tyroe Muhafidin, tempted by Sauron into becoming a Nazgnagôl. Nazgnagôl are men who wear one of Sauron’s Rings of Power, but still retain something of their humanity. That is, they are not fully Nazgûl, or Ringwraiths, as we know of the beings in the Third Age of J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth. They are, at this stage, Ring Servants.

Theo, last seen as a hopeful child of the Southlands and friend of hero elf Arondir, is now older and full of hate after five years of Númenórean oppression. Sauron sees something in him, something special, and offers Theo a gift. In Episode 2, appropriately called The Gift of Men, Sauron performs a dark ritual that lets Theo “meet” his mysterious father, or at least that’s what we think is happening here (with Sauron, you never really know!).

This is a callback to a scene in Season 1 where a young Theo encounters The Hilt, a broken sword-hilt forged during the First Age. It had been left hidden in a barn where Theo discovers it, and we see Theo’s blood drip into the Hilt, somehow feeding its regeneration. Clearly, Theo had some dark power inside him, although it was left unaddressed, sparking many fan theories over recent years.

In Season 3, Sauron notices the dark mark left on Theo’s arm after his interaction with The Hilt and immediately raises an eyebrow. Who was Theo’s father, really? During the ritual, Sauron uses the power of necromancy to communicate with the dead in the Unseen World. Sauron listens to the words of the dead, and tells Theo his father was named Fäldred, Son of Hammethreg. Theo asks, “Who are you, father?” The response, in Black Speech, is “Gorthmundur.” Sauron tells Theo this was a “Noble House of old, the sworn stewards of Mordor blessed with… certain powers.”

These powers, it seems, were passed down to Theo. “There is a reason you were drawn to that hilt, and it to you,” Sauron continues, before suggesting that Theo might have become ruler of the Southlands had his mother not “hidden the truth.” Theo responds to say his mother told him his father left. Sauron disputes this, before issuing a revelation that sends Theo spiralling: his mother murdered his father over what he had become.

Sauron, ever the opportunist, offers Theo a Ring of Power. He tells him that he has the power within him to become “a conqueror, a sorcerer, a king.” The downcast Theo accepts the gift.

Fast forward to Episode 4, and one of two shock deaths that punctuate this first block of The Rings of Power Season 3. Theo, now in full Nazgnagôl gear and spurred on by Sauron, murders his friend Arondir during the escape from Gundabad. It’s a shocking twist that cements Theo’s descent into darkness, and marks the end of the road for one of the mighty heroes of The Rings of Power.

In the interview below, I ask Tyroe Muhafidin about Theo’s journey in these first four episodes, what it’s like to play a Nazgnagôl, and where the murder of Arondir leaves The Rings of Power. And yes, we get into the question of Theo’s parentage. Was Sauron telling him the truth about his father?

IGN: The first question is an obvious one: how does it feel to be playing a Nazgnagôl?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was crazy. The costume automatically gives you a sense of such great strength and power. The biggest thing for me was, as soon as I put on those gauntlets there was an automatic transforming moment for me where you could just feel the power through your body. And it's interesting because I went from playing basically a helpless child to some godlike being. So it was a real jump and I had to do a lot of work in terms of my physicality and trying to look powerful and strong, which was something so new to me because I've always been scrawny and helpless. So yeah, it was a challenge, but I think I got there in the end, and I'm super, super grateful that I've got a chance to be something so iconic and to play something so iconic.

IGN: What is your understanding of what Nazgnagôl are, as it was explained to you?

Tyroe Muhafidin: So a Nazgûl directly translates to Ringwraith, whereas Nazgnagôl directly translates to Ring Servant. At this point in time when we've just put the ring on, we're not quite wraiths yet. We are still human men with autonomy over their body and can make their own decisions. We're just a lot stronger now. We've got a lot of power and a lot of dark power.

An important thing to know is at the beginning of this season, the One Ring hasn't yet been made. So these rings are yet to be binded completely to Sauron's will, where we are not now complete, I guess, his minions. We still have autonomy over who we are. That was the fun thing to play in this season, the gradual descent into more and more madness and more and more evil and darkness. But at this point in time, we get to very much still be people, just very strong people, I guess.

IGN: There's a really interesting scene where Sauron reveals Theo's parentage to him. What's your understanding of who Theo's father is? Sauron is suggesting at that moment that Theo has an innate power as a result of his parentage, but it's left ambiguous. And Sauron looks emotional even as he's talking to Theo about this. I almost was thinking he almost looks at him as his own son in some ways. So what's your read on that? What can you tell us about what all that means?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It's revealed that his father was the head of a few dark sorcerers and he sided with the dark side a long time ago, alongside his peers and the other Southlanders who sided with Sauron. And so there's that kind of information that's brought out.

But I think the big thing for Theo is when Sauron says his mother killed him when she found out. And I think that moment for me, and I think for Theo as a whole, it kind of sends a spin in the works of, what is Sauron really doing here and what is he trying to accomplish? Is he just trying to say words to make Theo happy, trying to build this broken boy up? Because he can see something for sure. And I don't think Theo really realizes. But I think there was always a dark side to Theo and maybe it was inherited, but that relationship to the Hilt was always something that stuck with him.

And I think maybe when he got a taste of that darkness in the Hilt, maybe it was the first time he kind of felt the presence of his father, and maybe that's why it was so addictive, that feeling to him. So I think this season we find out a little bit more of where he comes from.

But I think the biggest thing is, how much of it is the truth? What is Sauron saying that is manipulation and deceit and what is the truth? Which I think is kind of the fun dynamic of those scenes, is you feel like you're finding out a lot, but are you really?

IGN: There is a big moment in Episode 4 where Theo kills Arondir, a character who's been in the series from the beginning. When you first found out you'd be doing that, what was your reaction?

Tyroe Muhafidin: It was interesting. I was excited because I was like, "Oh, this is some juicy stuff to get into." But I think the moment I got the script, I found out and I was really excited because it was going to be some really cool stuff. When I read it all, it all became very real for me. And it was like, "Wow, this is a big task. This is super daunting." And there were months of intense anxiety coming up to this moment. But yeah, I guess I was just super excited, but anxious at the same time. And I feel like I knew at some point something big like this was going to happen. So I think it was just a matter of being prepared for it and trying to service Ismail [Cruz Córdova, who plays Arondir] as well, the best I possibly could.

IGN: What do you think the character death means for the show at that point and the story it's telling, but also for Theo? Do you see it as this is a moment that we see a tipping point in him that the audience is like, "Okay, yes, he has really gone too far."

Tyroe Muhafidin: In terms of the show, it's a moment of no-one is safe and there's no mercy from the dark side. And this war is very much real. The most talented and bravest of your warriors will go down. And that's kind of, I think, setting the premise for the rest of the war that's going to go on.

I think for Theo specifically, it definitely was that tipping point where his decision is made and his destiny is decided. And I think he realizes this afterwards as well, and whether he agrees with that decision he's made or not, he's made that decision.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power Season 3 episodes 1-4 are out now on Prime Video. Check back with IGN after Episodes 5 and 6 are released this week for more.

articles.content: Two decades later, this spectacle from Battlestar Galactica season 3’s “Exodus, Part 2” remains unforgettable sci-fi TV. It’s dazzling and horrifying, and still one of the coolest things ever broadcast on science-fiction television. From a tactical standpoint, the “Adama Maneuver” is absolutely bonkers and one of the riskiest spaceship tactics, perhaps ever (sorry, Vice-Admiral Holdo). Somehow, it’s also not even the most visually impressive sequence in the episode.

articles.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
articles.description: Accessing banned content is as easy as whipping out a thesaurus, Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee hears
articles.content:
Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

"I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.

"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently."

McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.

"And we know your algorithm would."

Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too.

Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.

She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.

There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

"So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content."

Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.

With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.

Success of user reports trails away

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.

Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly.

Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.

Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.

"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

articles.title: James Gunn Shuts Down Rumors That Skydance Is Meddling With Man of Tomorrow
articles.description: James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit.
articles.content:
James Gunn has shut down rumors that the new DC overseers at Skydance have meddled with his cut of Man of Tomorrow following his shocking DC Studios exit.

The internet has filled with gossip in the wake of Gunn and Peter Safran's departure as co-chairmen of the comic book entertainment wing earlier this week. As an ocean of rumors rises, some of the more worrying claims have seen some suggest Skydance has already taken control of the Superman director's sequel, which could result in major characters like Supergirl and Blue Beetle being cut entirely.

These are just some of the accusations that Gunn sought to dispel in a Threads post tonight. In what is essentially his first public statement since leaving DC Studios, the filmmaker took aim at the gossip that has DCU fans concerned. Not only have "sweeping changes" to Man of Tomorrow not been made, but apparently, no one at Skydance has even seen his movie yet.

"There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen Man of Tomorrow and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made," he said. "No one from Skydance has even seen the movie - the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false."

It's a response that will not answer every question comic book movie enjoyers have about the future of the DCU, but it does clear the air about much of the more damning chatter online. Gunn's comments mean that any talk of Skydance being unhappy with the current cut of Man of Tomorrow is false. It also sounds like, at least for now, Supergirl and Blue Beetle, who had been previously reported to return, are safe.

With so much time left before David Corenswet's Clark Kent returns to theaters in July, though, it's hard to say how the Skydance takeover may impact its release. It's best to wait until Gunn or Skydance has more to share before setting any firm expectations in place for now.

All of that said, it's not too hard to see why fans of the DCU have felt uneasy in the last few days. Gunn and Safran have orchestrated the DCU to tell a varied collection of superpowered stories for four years, with its overarching plan for the years ahead only just starting to come into view. Pulling them from the driver's seat means the future is more unknown than ever before, especially considering Skydance was quick to find a replacement in Marvel alum Jeremy Latcham.

Will Man of Tomorrow be altered against Gunn's will? Will Skydance reboot the DC movie universe and scrap future plans for the DCU? How will any of this affect future entries in Robert Pattinson's The Batman saga? It's all too soon to tell, but that won't stop the rumor mill from pushing ahead.

What we do know is what Gunn shared with fans in the immediate aftermath of his exit. In a letter posted to social media, he promised that the characters he and Safran helped set up "will live on." He also confirmed that the duo was recently "engaged on another DC project" that he is writing. What that project is remains a mystery.

For more on the future of the DCU, you can read up on what we know about Latcham. You can also check out another report that suggested Skydance intends to prioritize more well-known heroes in the DC portfolio going forward. Man of Tomorrow, meanwhile, is set to premiere July 9, 2027.

articles.title: After Another Year of Price Hikes, What Streaming Deals Will We Get for Black Friday 2026?
articles.content:
We’re officially in the thick of deals season, and if there’s one thing I personally spend way too much money on, it’s streaming subscriptions. It doesn't help that everyone keeps hiking prices, and deals are rarer than ever.

Thankfully, there’s one time of year where you can often get a decent amount of those very subscriptions for much cheaper than usual: Black Friday.

Almost every service is likely to drop some type of deal, though the majority will be on ad-supported plans. If you’ve been intrigued by any particular service, or want to strategize some free trials and cancellations, here’s what streaming deals I expect we’ll see for Black Friday this year.

Black Friday Streaming Deal Predictions

In general, deals will certainly be live from Black Friday (November 27) to Cyber Monday (November 30). However, some services may launch their Black Friday deals in the week before the main event.

Amazon Prime Video

Starting from the top, obviously Amazon will be all over Black Friday (check out the retailer’s full sale schedule). Prime Video is included in Amazon memberships, which pretty much never go on sale. The service does offer a 30-day free trial and a hefty 50% discount for anyone under the age of 25.

Channel Add-Ons, however, like AMC+ and Britbox, will likely have deals through Prime Video in addition to their own platforms. Amazon’s general Black Friday sale starts November 19, but I imagine most Add-On discounts will appear on Black Friday proper.

Disney+ and Hulu

Disney+ has always launched some sort of Black Friday deal, but as we’ve seen across streaming, the discounts have gotten less generous over time.

Last year, Black Friday came right after Disney+ rolled out a price hike. The Black Friday deal only applied to the ad-supported bundle of both services, dropping the monthly price from $12.99 to $4.99 for a full 12 months.

Disney+ increased prices again back in September, but the Hulu bundle actually stayed at $12.99. I’d guess we see the return of the $4.99 deal on the ad-supported bundle for a full 12-month window, but there’s a chance it only goes down to $5.99 to align with the new Disney+ pricing.

HBO Max

HBO Max is in a particularly weird place. Paramount finalized its acquisition of Warner Bros. earlier this year, and indicated early on in negotiations they were planning to merge their streaming services. More recently, Paramount announced that HBO Max and Paramount+ will be getting a new streaming bundle in early 2027, which is likely a first step on the path to a full merger.

However, that doesn’t mean Black Friday deals are off the table. Last year, HBO Max offered a particularly generous deal, dropping the ad-supported plan to just $2.99/month for a 12-month period. We’ll likely see the same deal return this year, though potentially limited to six or even two months as HBO Max navigates a more uncertain future.

Paramount+

Paramount+ is in a similar boat to HBO Max, but I’m a bit more confident in this one, largely because Paramount+ has offered relatively consistent deals even as other services have shied away from them. Right now, for example, you can get 50% off an annual subscription using a promo code.

For Black Friday, Paramount+ will likely offer a two-month subscription deal on both of its ad-supported and ad-free Showtime plans. Yep, we might actually have an ad-free deal on our hands. In 2025, Paramount+ dropped the prices of both subscriptions to $2.99/month, and given the consistency of deals since then, I expect to see the same deal return for 2026.

Apple TV

Speaking of ad-free, praise be Apple TV. Apple’s streaming service keeps it simple with one ad-free subscription plan, so if you’re dead set on picking up a new service without ads, this is your best bet.

Last year, Apple TV dropped the price of its subscription from $12.99 to $5.99/month for a six-month period. Since then, however, the service hiked prices by $2 for a standard monthly rate of $14.99. With that in mind, I expect to see the return of at least a six-month deal period, but the discount might be closer to $6.99 to hit the same discount percentage.

Peacock

Peacock was actually one of the only streaming services that didn’t offer any Black Friday deal in 2025. That doesn’t mean we’re out of luck this year, but it isn’t a great sign, especially given the service just hiked prices again this Summer.

If you desperately want to catch up on Peacock’s sitcoms and reality TV lineup, I recommend keeping an eye out for deals on Walmart+ subscriptions. This is basically Walmart’s version of Amazon Prime, but it also includes Peacock Premium, and often get 50% discounts during major sales events.

articles.title: Blade Runner 2099 Executive Producers Confirm Franchise Owners Are in Talks for AAA Video Game Adaptation
articles.description: Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, executive producers for Blade Runner 2099 and co-CEOs of Alcon Entertainment, have confirmed that they are in discussions to create a AAA video game based on the iconic cyberpunk franchise.
articles.content:
Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, executive producers for Blade Runner 2099 and co-CEOs of Alcon Entertainment, the owner of the Blade Runner franchise, have confirmed that they are in discussions to create a AAA video game based on the iconic cyberpunk IP.

I got the chance to chat with Kosove and Johnson ahead of Blade Runner 2099’s release on Prime Video later this month. During our conversation, I brought up the wildly successful Cyberpunk 2077, wondering why Blade Runner hasn’t had a similar AAA game made after it and if any conversations have been had about finally giving this IP a major modern video game release.

“Yes,” Kosove confirmed, and emphasized the phrase “AAA,” making it clear that Alcon has a grand vision for Blade Runner’s future in the gaming space. Of course, he couldn’t tell me much more, but impressed upon the importance of allowing players to “interact” with the world of Blade Runner in this hypothetical game.

This is big news for fans of Blade Runner and the cyberpunk genre, in general. While Blade Runner has enjoyed its status as a cult-classic and cornerstone of modern science fiction, it hasn’t exactly been blessed in the game department.

Based on IGN’s own list of Blade Runner games, the franchise has four licensed titles. The first, published in 1985 by CRL Group PLC for the Commodore 64, is an absolute dinosaur of a game that wasn’t well-received even at the time of its release. In the game, players hunt down replicants (here, replidroids) for bounty money. Due to the cost of movie rights at the time, this game was said to merely be “inspired” by the "Vangelis soundtrack" of Ridley Scott’s 1982 film and not a direct adaptation.

The next Blade Runner game, which was released in 1997, enjoyed far more critical acclaim and is still considered a classic to this day. Developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin Interactive, this point-and-click adventure title was one of the very first titles to use 3D character models and real-time environments. A remake was released in 2022.

Another game, titled Blade Runner 2033: Labyrinth, was announced in 2023 and developed by Annapurna Interactive. Unfortunately, the project is now largely considered to be canceled, having been delisted from Steam and removed from Annapurna’s website. (Blade Runner 2049: Replicant Pursuit was released in 2017. It was a short, tie-in VR experience meant to promote the second film, but not a full, official game.)

Given that it’s been nearly 30 years since Blade Runner fans have had a fresh, critically acclaimed video game adaptation, this latest news is extremely exciting and opens up an entire world of possibilities. And considering Kosove’s focus on player interactivity and AAA quality, it sounds like Alcon has a clear vision for what it wants this game to be — and I can’t wait to see what they come up with.

Blade Runner 2099 releases on Prime Video on November 25.

Sony has confirmed Marvel's Spider-Man 2, Arc Raiders, and four more games are receiving QSSR support on base PS5s.

The list of six newcomers joining the small-but-growing group of supported games was unveiled in a PlayStation.Blog post. In addition to confirmation that incoming updates will add QSSR (Quick Spectral Super Resolution), the post included testimonials from each of the studios' developers, who shared how the tech will impact visuals.

When Sony pulled back the curtain on QSSR in October, it came with confirmation that it had already been implemented in Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yōtei. Now, we know that Insomniac's Marvel's Spider-Man 2, Remedy Entertainment's Control Resonant, Embark Studios' Arc Raiders and The Finals, Hello Games' No Man's Sky, and Expression Games' Hell Let Loose: Vietnam will soon take advantage of the AI upscaling tech.

"Having seen great results integrating QSSR in Marvel’s Wolverine, our team decided to bring it to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 as well, in an update that’s live now!" Insomniac head of technology Mike Fitzgerald said. "We’re excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see QSSR’s exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both Fidelity and Performance modes."

Remedy said QSSR will bring noticeable improvements in image stability and fine detail when it launches in a new update in December. Hello Games founder Sean Murray, meanwhile, promised that players can look forward to No Man's Sky looking "sharper, cleaner, and more beautiful" at the "best possible framerate" in the next few weeks. "With the new QSSR coming soon to ARC Raiders and The Finals, we can deliver increased sharpness, better environmental clarity, and overall visual improvements to even more PlayStation players," Embark said. "We are very happy to see Sony’s continued investment in PlayStation technology translate into meaningful improvements for all players, bringing more immersive experiences across the PlayStation ecosystem."

articles.title: Before Directing the Biggest Success of His Career, Steven Spielberg Almost Made an Alien Horror Movie Instead
articles.description: Before directing E.T., Steven Spielberg almost made an alien horror movie called Night Skies.
articles.content:
In the late 1970s/early 1980s, Steven Spielberg was developing a movie that ultimately would never get made. And yet, from a different perspective, it actually would get made… as a bunch of other, quite famous films. We’re talking Gremlins. We’re talking Poltergeist. And we’re talking E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial.

“It was a dream team of people working on this thing. It was going to be a horror movie about these evil aliens, or mischievous aliens, that come to this rural farmstead and really mess with this family – they really fuck with this family,” explains movie journalist and author Max Evry, who just released a book about the film called Stranded on Earth: How Night Skies Became E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial.

Dream team is putting it lightly, as Night Skies had Spielberg producing, John Sayles scripting, production illustrator Ron Cobb expected to make his directorial debut, and Rick Baker designing the aliens. And of course, Kathleen Kennedy was also onboard, as she was working for Spielberg at this point in her career and would soon get her first full producer credit on E.T.

I recently spoke to Evry, who is also an occasional contributor to IGN – and who you may recall was also the author of that very popular book about David Lynch’s Dune, A Masterpiece in Disarray, from a couple of years back. We discussed how Night Skies went from alien horror movie to the family-friendly mega-hit that was E.T., how Poltergeist and Gremlins were born alongside its development, and how Stranded on Earth is, as the author puts it, “a hard R-rated book about a children's movie.”

From Close Encounters to a ‘Famous Clusterfuck’... to E.T.

Stranded on Earth begins with a look back at Spielberg’s earliest filmmaking endeavors as a teen, including a film called Firelight which he made for $500 and which actually got a theatrical release – in the wunderkind’s hometown for one night, at least (the director’s semi-autobiographical film The Fabelmans recreates this moment from his life). The film was an early example of Spielberg’s interest in UFOs and the creatures behind them.

“We're dealing with Spielberg, we're dealing with aliens, so we got to go all the way back to when he was 15, 16, making his first sort of feature film,” says Evry. “It was like this two-hour epic that he made when he was a teenager, and that story is really fun. It sets up the way that Spielberg deals with aliens throughout his career, because it's like Martin Scorsese and gangsters. Spielberg has used aliens as a vessel for whatever kind of creative mood he happens to be in. I don't believe – and there are many people who corroborate this in the book – he has a firm belief one way or the other about alien visitations and things like that. I think it's just a great tool that he uses to explore different subjects.”

'1941 was a nightmare production... It hurt Spielberg's reputation a lot, and it sort of showed he wasn't bulletproof.' Of course, Spielberg would have great success with 1977’s Close Encounters of the Third Kind, and the book recounts the filmmaker’s less than enthusiastic plans for a direct sequel to that film. That’s where Night Skies comes into the picture.

“They spent close to a million dollars developing this thing. Some people in the book described it as kind of a weird science experiment, like maybe it'll go, maybe it won't. But it was heavily developed, and I think would've been a great movie,” says Evry.

This was all going on during a very memorable time for Spielberg, because he also had the infamous misfire 1941, a World War II-era comedy starring an ensemble that included John Belushi, hit theaters in 1979. As Evry puts it, the film was “a famous clusterfuck … a nightmare production where he was essentially going crazy with this thing, and it just kept getting bigger and bigger and bigger. … It hurt his reputation a lot, and it sort of showed he wasn't bulletproof.”

The fallout from 1941 would impact how Night Skies – and then as it morphed into what would become E.T. – was viewed by the studios.

“There were a lot of people who thought he might be done,” he says. “So even after this project evolved from Night Skies to E.T., it became almost like this nuclear football where Columbia had it and then they just decided they didn't want it and they gave it to Universal. Universal was kind of like, ‘Eh. We'll do it, but you have to raise the money through a bond company. We don't want to directly fund it because we don't want to be responsible if you go over budget again.’ It was this interesting period where it was like the last time people didn't trust Steven Spielberg.”

Evolution of an Idea, From Aliens to Ghosts to Gremlins

Spielberg was never going to direct Night Skies, and in fact it was during this period that he began to produce other directors’ films, the earliest examples being Robert Zemeckis’ I Wanna Hold Your Hand (1978) and Used Cars (1980). Zemeckis, with his partner Bob Gale, also worked on a script for Spielberg at one point called After School, “and that had a lot of elements that carried forward into E.T. also,” says Evry. “So it's not just Night Skies. It was sort of [Spielberg] blending After School with Night Skies, and that's how you get E.T.”

But before that, when Night Skies was still Night Skies, it was Ron Cobb who was going to direct the film.

“It was going to be his debut, and he developed it from the ground up,” says Evry. “There's some false information out there that it was between Cobb and Tobe Hooper. That is not true. Basically, Tobe Hooper came in much later when Cobb was ensconced in Spain doing the production design for Conan the Barbarian, and he couldn't come back and work on Night Skies. Rick Baker's doing storyboards for the film without him. I think at that point, Spielberg calls up Tobe Hooper and is like, ‘Hey, I've got this alien project. Are you interested in directing it?’ Tobe Hooper was like, ‘Nah, but I'd like to do a movie about ghosts.’”

There are even some lines from the Night Skies scripts which can be found in Poltergeist – 'They’re here…' for example. And of course, that project became Poltergeist. Evry explains that while many film fans think that Night Skies fed into Poltergeist, the two projects were really in parallel development.

“They were happening at the exact same time, and that's interesting because they're both about essentially these families with the same makeup, like mom, dad, three kids, one older, one younger, one very young,” he says. “And the focal point is on the youngest one, and you've got this supernatural force encroaching upon their house. In one case, it's ghosts. In one case, it's aliens.”

There are even some lines from the Night Skies scripts which can be found in Poltergeist – “They’re here…” for example.

In Evry’s view, Gremlins has a lot more of Night Skies in it though. While Gremlins originated as a spec script by Chris Columbus, John Sayles took over as a ghost writer after Columbus. And Sayles was also the main writer behind Night Skies.

“So that is where you start to see some crossover and some of the similar ideas,” says Evry. “I mean, even down to the fact that Night Skies was inspired by this ‘real incident’ called the Kelly-Hopkinsville Incident of 1955, which was aliens attacking a farm. It's a famous thing in UFO-logy, and there's a whole chapter about it in the book.” (Evry even visited Hopkinsville for his research.)

That’s where the term “little green men” comes from, and as Evry points out, at the end of Gremlins they refer to the little creatures as little green men.

“If you look at the actual eyewitness drawings of the aliens from Kelly-Hopkinsville, they look a hell of a lot like the Gremlins,” adds the author.

A Painful Memory

For Evry, the key creative force behind Night Skies that he wanted to talk to was legendary makeup effects creator Rick Baker. But for Baker, this was a project that elicited a lot of painful memories.

“In some ways, he's the central figure and it's the most dramatic element of the book,” says Evry. “John Sayles and Ron Cobb, they both came out of it just fine. But for Rick, it was a really tough experience, which we talk about – for whatever reason, he and Spielberg just had this tremendous falling out, very dramatic. And it was a trauma for him. And it's like, I never wanted to portray seven-time Oscar winner Rick Baker as some kind of victim, but the thing you have to remember is at that time he was zero-Oscar winner Rick Baker. He was still kind of new to the business.”

It seems Spielberg has his own take on what went down between him and Baker on Night Skies, and it doesn’t necessarily match with how Baker remembers it.

“There's another book about E.T. where Spielberg – I didn't put this in my book because I thought it was embarrassing – his quote was, ‘Rick and I decided this was not the project we were going to work on,’” says Evry. “If you read [my] book, you'll have a different feeling about that quote. But Rick, he was very honest and he was very candid, which was so great to hear him talk about it. And I talked to other people who were in his studio as well, and they corroborate everything he says.”

'Spielberg has this intuitive creativity where he just said, You know what? I think I can do something else with this.' Baker was actually working on An American Werewolf in London at the same time that he was on Night Skies, and of course that film would go on to be an incredible breakthrough success in large part due to Baker’s effects work.

“An important thing to note is you've seen American Werewolf, and you know how innovative that was,” says Evry. “And I am here to tell you that his work on Night Skies was just as good, if not better. I actually discovered the original VHS Night Skies alien test that he did that he sent to Spielberg, and it's unbelievable. If you did it today, it would still stand up. And this is far and away ahead of anything being done in makeup effects in 1980. The alien was so expressive, so versatile. It was really cool. It was really eerie.” (You can check out a glimpse of it here.)

Of course, that’s the trick with any history lesson – whose memories are correct, who has embellished a story, knowingly or not, and where does what really happened come to the forefront? Evry says that’s part of the fun of his book, as it gets into a sort of “Rashomon, where there's a chapter on John Sayles, there's a chapter on Ron Cobb, there's a chapter on Rick Baker, and you start to see the story from different angles.”

Of course, one undeniable aspect to it all is that at some point, Spielberg decided to make E.T. instead.

“Spielberg has this intuitive creativity where he just said, ‘You know what? I think I can do something else with this,’” says Evry. “I'm really excited for horror fans, science fiction fans, but especially Spielberg fans to come away from this book with just a totally different perspective on what E.T. is, on what it could have been, and on what came after.”

articles.title: FAA lifts ground stop after hours-long delays snag travelers
articles.description: Safety reasons and unspecified communications issue cited
articles.content:
The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. The FAA has not yet confirmed a reason for the stop.

Original story below:

"The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement.

The FAA ATCSCC advisory halts departing flights and says international flights will be dealt with individually.

The notice says, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis."

Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now."

An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage."

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities.

The grounding follows on the heels of a major Microsoft outage that has affected many Microsoft-hosted services, particularly email, for more than 24 hours so far. There's no indication presently that the two incidents are related.

We'll update this story as more information becomes available.®

Updated at 0211 Saturday UTC to reflect the lifting of the ground stop.

Updated to add at 2353 UTC

CBS News reports that “an update to the private communications network that connects America’s air traffic control system caused the system to reboot. When the FAA’s telecommunication infrastructure rebooted, it crashed, causing the communications outage. The system is operated by L3Harris.”

L3Harris has not responded to a request for comment.

Updated to add at 2340 UTC

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), awarded the FAA’s $875 million, 12-year contract for its new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system, has issued a statement asserting that its products played no role in the FAA’s flight suspension. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

articles.title: Kevin Feige Didn't Want Wanda in VisionQuest Because He Was Worried She Would 'Distract' From the Core Show
articles.description: Marvel actor Paul Bettany has said Kevin Feige didn't want Elizabeth Olsen's Wanda Maximoff to be in VisionQuest because he was worried she might "distract" from the show's core.
articles.content:
Marvel actor Paul Bettany has said Kevin Feige didn't want Elizabeth Olsen's Wanda Maximoff to be in VisionQuest because he was worried she might "distract" from the show's core.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe star recalled the conversation he had with the Marvel Studios bigwig when speaking with The Playlist. MCU followers spent the months leading up to the new Disney+ offshoot speculating about how it may serve as a vehicle for an unlikely resurrection.

Those who have kept up with the nearly 20-year-old cinematic universe will remember that Wanda met her end in the closing moments of 2022's Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. She's yet to be seen since, and although discussions about seeing her share a screen with Vision were had, Bettany said it was an idea Feige was never too fond of.

"There were questions about it, whether that should happen, whether it opened up too much for the MCU, whether they wanted to do it later," he remembered. "I don't know. But I remember having this conversation with [Kevin], and he said, 'You and Terry have done such a great job at making me care about Vision. I really don’t think you should distract from that by giving the audience that at the end of the [show].

"It will just fundamentally all become about WandaVision again, and this should and can stand on its own.' And I think he was right."

The main events of VisionQuest came and went without any signs that Olsen had recorded new footage to fit directly within VisionQuest, leaving the MCU without a proper family reunion. It was a disappointing moment for those who had spent months speculating she would reappear ahead of Avengers: Doomsday as theories were finally put to rest.

Warning! Spoilers for VisionQuest's finale credits scenes follow.

If you've finished VisionQuest, you'll know that disappointment didn't last long. Just as the final credits for the finale episode came to an end, viewers were taken back to Wanda's resting place on the snowy cliffs of Mount Wundagore. There, a cloaked figure that looks and sounds a lot like Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom reaches out to her, saying, "Scarlet Witch, awaken. Your power will be mine." Then, her eyes open.

Yes, Olsen and Wanda Maximoff are coming back, with the return set up alongside VisionQuest's finale, despite Feige's wishes. To be fair, the reveal mostly seemed to consist of reused footage from her appearance in the Doctor Strange sequel. The scene is also just about as far removed from VisionQuest itself as it can be. So, while Feige may have wanted to avoid Wanda distracting from the partial family reunion we got in VisionQuest, her inclusion at least managed to arrive long after the main story wrapped up.

We'll hopefully know more about Wanda's future – and hopefully whether or not she'll reunite with Vision, Billy, and Tommy – when Avengers: Doomsday premieres next month, December 18. Until then, you can check out what IGN thought of VisionQuest's finale in our 7/10 review.

"The last-minute addition of a new villain derails the finale of VisionQuest somewhat," we said, "but the series still succeeds where Vision and Ultron are concerned."

articles.title: Barbie Rewind Review
articles.content:
Barbie Rewind feels like the equivalent of showing your children the family heirloom rocking horse, and then watching them poke it and ask if they can play Roblox. A weird mix of nostalgia and interior decorating sim, it's home to 17 retro Barbie games and a dreamhouse to arrange Barbie-appropriate furniture in. Now, it's been over three decades since I last smashed a Barbie against a G.I. Joe and made smooching noises, so I called in two gaming experts, Kora (9) and Paloma (5), to assist with this review. Sadly, unlike her looks, time has not been kind to Barbie's gaming legacy.

Why does she have a scuba mask but not a toilet? "That doesn't make sense. Why does she have a scuba mask but not a toilet?" A crucial question from Kora as the girls got stuck into the only bit of Barbie Rewind they actually cared about: the decorating. This might be selling itself as a collection of Barbie games from 1991's NES Barbie through to 2007's Barbie as the Island Princess, but its newly created Dreamhouse mode is the big winner here. There are more than 250 pieces of furniture, and some of them are unlocked by playing the retro Barbie games. The big B and other characters like Ken and Christie give you quests, but they're just to decorate the house, so it's a bit like someone saying "be careful" when you're already falling down the stairs.

The Barbie games themselves got what I would call a polite fiddle. I played all of them before the expert advisors were called in, and Rewind is heavy on minigames of the platforming and "catch the falling coconut" variety. These games haven't been given the Monkey Island-style reboot; they're presented seemingly entirely as is, but with a frame that relates to their various consoles to help smooth over any aspect ratio issues.

It's great as a museum piece, but show it to anyone born after 2010 and they basically look like cave paintings. "Is that meant to be Barbie?" asks Kora incredulously, squinting at Barbie Pet Rescue. Paloma picks up the controller to play one of the minigames, a sort of cat Pong using two paws that is apparently essential to pet care, and watches the ball of yarn awkwardly bounce off the screen. She knows controllers, she plays Lego Batman, but this minigame makes no sense. The ball is slow, the angles are off, and Paloma looks at me exasperated as if I personally offended her.

Controls were an issue throughout, changing between games in a way that meant looking up the button layout for everything they wanted to try. One smart addition is the option to tweak things like your total health in certain games, which makes for a less stressful experience all round. The girls liked the concept of a lot of them – veterinarian duties, horse racing, and the fashion dress-up doll in particular – but these are kids born long after the time when you knew that what you saw on the cover of a game was light years away from how it actually looked. I could burn through pixelated bouncing and stilted dialogue on nostalgia alone, but Kora and Paloma are playing Hogwarts Legacy; they have iPad games, and their eyes know not the trauma of staring into a Gameboy Color in the back of a moving vehicle.

articles.title: Some of These GTA 6 Clips Look So Good That I Don't Care if It's Running at 30fps
articles.description: Earlier this week, Rockstar confirmed that GTA 6 would be running at 30fps on all of the consoles, including the PS5 Pro. And while I wasn't surprised, I've been watching some of the clips that have been trickling out this week, and I can't say I'm not excited to play it, even at 30fps.
articles.content:
This is an opinion piece by Jackie Thomas, IGN's Senior Tech Editor who has been writing about PC hardware for more than a decade.

Earlier this week, Rockstar confirmed that GTA 6 would be running at 30fps on all of the consoles, including the PS5 Pro. And while I wasn't surprised, I've been watching some of the clips that have been trickling out this week, and I can't say I'm not excited to play it, even at 30fps.

The one that really got my attention is this one from Instagram account onlyindade. It's a simple clip of some cars slowly driving down the road, but it looks downright incredible. I've been staring at high-end graphics for 20 years, and even I had to do a double take to make sure it wasn't just real-life footage. The footage is highly compressed and it's hard to make out some of the details, but even with compression artifacts, you can tell GTA 6 is going to be an absolutely stunning game.

Pausing the video and looking at the road, the texture quality is incredible. You can make out individual bumps in the asphalt, along with little pieces of debris on the side of the road. Looking at the cars themselves, the reflections in the cars' paint are beautiful and make it look like an actual material. The shadows, too, are nice and soft and behave similarly to how you'd expect the actual shadows of the cars to behave, leaning away from where the sun is.

These clips from onlyindade don't specify which platform they were captured on, but I'd put my money on the PS5 Pro. In its blog earlier this week, Rockstar said the PS5 Pro would have PSSR upscaling and ray traced shadows that are exclusive to that console. Looking at the shadows cast by the cars in that clip, along with the lack of aliasing on the distant buildings – which admittedly might be drowned out by compression blurriness – it definitely looks like PSSR helped quite a bit.

Onlyindade shared another clip, this time with the camera inside of a car and looking out the window as it drives down the street. Just like in the first clip, the textures on the car door are pristine, and just straight-up look real. Later on in the clip, when whoever's behind the camera is walking on the sidewalk, the camera looks at a blue and pink car that looks like it came straight out of the '50s.

In that part of the scene, it's not the car that impresses me, but rather the shadows cast from the palm tree above it. Again, this clip is super compressed, but you can make out individual leaves in the shadows. There's also a character standing next to the car on his phone, and the shadows there look phenomenal and even move flawlessly as he does.

When looking at these clips, it's important to keep in mind that both the PS5 and the Xbox Series X are running on graphics architectures that are going on 7 years old at this point. It doesn't help that those graphics chips are paired with CPUs that are just as old. Even with that aging hardware, it sure seems like Rockstar was able to craft something that looks better than any other game on the market right now.

Maybe it was just my internet connection, but all of the clips shared by that Dade County Instagram account are extremely compressed, and so it's very possible that some red flags were grayed out. In a huge open world like this with long draw distances, the detail on distant objects is usually the first thing to fall, especially as the game runs out of VRAM budget.

In that first clip, it looks like the edges of distant objects are going to be crisp, but the compression artifacts make those kinds of details seem wobbly no matter how good they look. There's a decent chance that when I boot this game up on my PS5 Pro at launch, I'm going to be assaulted by jagged edges on distant streetlights and buildings – and that is one of my pet peeves. But it doesn't look like that's the case. I just hope I haven't been fooled by online compression.

More than anything, these clips confirm that 60fps was probably out of the question for the current-generation consoles. With this level of fidelity, I'm just surprised it's running at all. But the one thought that keeps bouncing around in my head is, "Just how good will this look when I can run it on an RTX 5090 and a 9800X3D?" Now I just have to sit and wait for Rockstar to port the game. Hopefully the rumors about the PC port coming out next year are true.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering’s Star Trek Commander Precons Ranked: Why We Are the Borg Takes the Top Spot
articles.description: We ranked all four Magic: The Gathering Star Trek Commander precons—from Picard’s Federation Fleet to We Are the Borg—by gameplay, value, and key reprints.
articles.content:
Magic: The Gathering’s Star Trek set is finally here, closing out a particularly packed release schedule for Wizards of the Coast’s long-running TCG.

Star Trek is the seventh set of the year, and it brings with it another four Commander decks to take this year’s total to 17. Still, as we all know, not all decks are created equal - so which one comes out on top?

The Klingons or the Borg? Picard or Spock? Here’s our ranking.

Before We Begin

If you’re picking up all four decks because you’re a Trekkie, or you just love new precons, Amazon has cut the price of the bundle again to just $224.97, basically offsetting the “Universes Beyond” tax.

That’s not the Collector Editions, though: Those are well over $100 each. They include the same cards, but all in foil.

Ranking Magic’s Star Trek Decks

Federation Fleet

Color Identity: Jeskai (blue, red, white)

Reprints of note: Alhammarret’s Archive

Magic loves to put heroic precons in Jeskai colors, and Federation Fleet is no exception - although it does come last in our ranking.

Its primary Commander, Jean-Luc Picard, Luminary, is a four-cost 2/4 that draws you cards as you play historic permanents, which then triggers the Seek Out mechanic. This lets you charge up a Spacecraft and add a counter to another target creature.

It’s not that it’s not a fun, cohesive deck, but it’s definitely just not as interesting on a mechanical level as the others in this set.

Klingon Fury

Color Identity: Mardu (white, black, red)

Reprints of note: Sword of Light, Shadow and World at War

Worf, Defiant Commander is in charge of the Klingon Fury deck, which makes use of the Battlefront mechanic to encourage players to play aggressively.

Worf creates Klingon Warrior tokens when it hits the battlefield, and the more opponents you attack on your turn, the more cards you exile from the top of your library, which you can play until the end of your next turn.

It’s not quite cheating big creatures into play, but it should mean you’re well-stocked with options as long as you keep Worf around.

Landing Party

Color Identity: Bant (green, white, blue)

Reprints of note: Ancient Greenwarden, Scute Swarm, Exploration, Heroic Intervention

Commander Spock is the logical choice for a Commander in Bant colors, and Wizards of the Coast has made it so here (sorry).

Landing Party’s Strange New Worlds mechanic helps play cards more quickly if you’ve got more differently named lands in the set. Given there are 40 in the deck, that should be easily done, but this deck also gives you a big bundle of non-basic lands in Bant colors if you need them.

Captain Kirk, Boldly Going, is another Commander option. William Shatner himself is a 3/4 with vigilance who powers up your Spacecraft cards. The card can also grab you land cards or the Enterprise from your library or graveyard.

We Are The Borg

Color Identity: Esper (white, blue, black)

Reprints of note: Toxic Deluge, Unwinding Clock, Morphic Pool

Our top pick for the Commander precons in the Star Trek set is We Are The Borg. Standing somewhere between artifact synergies and a “what’s yours is mine” deck, The Borg Queen pumps artifact creatures and also assimilates cards to your side of the battlefield.

Unwinding Clock is a very welcome reprint here since it fits nicely into just about any other artifact strategy, and Locutus of Borg can help you pull even more Borg to the table. It’s a deck that’s likely to get out of hand pretty quickly, and for that reason, it’s our top pick.

For more on Magic: The Gathering, check out some of our favorite Commander decks of all time, as well as the latest on reprints of the sought-after Universes Beyond: Warhammer 40K decks, and the most valuable cards to look out for in the new Star Trek Universes Beyond set.

articles.title: Tech Companies Are Trying to Shift the Entire Concept of Privacy (Again)
articles.description: Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did. Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intell
articles.content:
Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did.

Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants, rings, and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long.

Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps, collaborative software, or your cloud backup solutions, have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game.

Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. 

This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense.

Let’s break this down by looking at some of the biggest players currently in the game: Apple and Amazon, who have two different takes on transcribing audio throughout the day, as well as Meta and Google, who both have slapped AI and cameras onto eyeglasses. 

How to Think About the Technical Promises Companies Make

Ask Apple about privacy concerns and they’ll point to a white paper that explains all the technical barriers between them as a company and the data generated by the watch. Ask Meta and they’ll talk about all the ways you can customize the privacy controls or how certain details, like faces, may be blurred out when you interact with Meta AI through the glasses (but not during standard recording). Google does this too. Amazon will also talk about how you’re always in control, and no audio is stored (though it’ll also let you enable Amazon store integration, so your conversations can directly result in ads for products). And so on across all the companies making these products.

Some of these solutions do a better job than others at cutting out potential law enforcement or company access to this data. There will be a time to dive into these details more deeply, but the technical privacy promises these companies focus on only cover the consumer and user of the device. They ignore every bystander you interact with and their inability to actually opt out. There is no technical protection for you as a non-user of these devices, the person who finds yourself captured by them. 

Still, we hope to look deeper into the technical differences between this category of devices soon.

There Must Be Some Laws to Consider, Right?

With something like Apple’s Audio Intelligence and Amazon’s Bee devices, it may be best to treat them similar to an always-recording microphone, even if companies try to claim there’s “technically” no audio recording. These tools still often use a microphone to capture raw audio from conversations and convert it into summaries or transcripts before discarding the audio. Google's blog post notes that it has  whole responsible use part of their Terms of Service where users have to agree not to record others without permission or in sensitive places. 

But it’s not just the question of the legality from the point of view of the user. Law enforcement will eventually try to compel access to the data that these products create (either real-time audio or the summaries and transcripts they create). And while some products, like Apple’s Audio Intelligence, are engineered to make that difficult, not every product will be. We know from history that when data exists, governments will do everything they can to access it. There’s no reason to think something would change today.

No Tech and Legal Solutions Will Reduce Social Issues

There is a problem humming along in the background that is impossible to address with technical or legal solutions. If secretly documenting conversations becomes the norm, it makes every private conversation less spontaneous and open. It breaks a longstanding social norm that you will not record and document every conversation with friends, family, colleagues, or strangers. 

The companies that make these sorts of products like to claim they’re no different from tools we already have. You can easily record everything right now with a phone or a camera. Heck, you can do so with a camcorder or cassette recorder if you want. And you can transcribe conversations with pen and paper, too. But those are actionable steps we take that both require effort from the user, and are clear to others around us. This new wave of passive surveillance tech is designed to encourage continuous monitoring and hide its use. 

Even taken at face value, none of these products can understand the complex social context we all navigate every day. We intrinsically know there are different social agreements we all make when we’re standing on a street corner, at a protest, in a bathroom, at a doctor’s office, at the gym, or in a restaurant. Taking notes in a meeting at work is completely normal. Getting a summary of a conversation with your best friend about their divorce is not. Always-on monitoring of our conversations is an unacceptable burden on our conversational privacy. 

Google seems to all but admit this problem in a conversation with CNN when it described the company’s experiments with a notification system that would alert people’s phones when someone was recording nearby: 

“And just alerting bystanders doesn’t do much to help, [Juston Payne, senior director of product management at Google] said. “It can actually be weirdly disempowering to you in that you’re like, ‘What am I meant to do now?’” he said.”

What We Can Do About It

It’s easy to buy into the tech company line that these products are inevitable, but we’ve seen so many vaporware products over the years that we should take those claims of success with a grain of salt. We’ve seen entire product categories come and go within just a few years, and if the public doesn’t want this stuff, the tech companies will have to throw in the towel. 

Of course, that doesn’t mean we all just have to sit around and hope that’s what happens. For its part, Apple launched its Audio Intelligence features in beta specifically to get feedback, and we think it’s worth taking the time to fill out their feedback forms (or in the Feedback Assistant app if you’re in the beta) and let them know what you think.

Products from the likes of Meta, Google, Amazon, and others might be harder to push back on, but politely and clearly engaging with those who use them in ways that make you uncomfortable is a good place to start. And if you see abusive videos on social networks where these sorts of products are used, report them. If you find these products useful for yourself, make it clear to those around you when you’re using them, and only do so with consent and in social moments where it makes sense to do so.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.
